title: When London Closes Its River
cues: These silver structures sit across the Thames in London. A ship can pass between them. Yet before a dangerous tide reaches the city, the same stretch of open water can become a wall. Where are the gates?
To see why London needs them, follow the river east. It opens into the North Sea. The tide travels back up that opening, towards the city, while fresh water from inland is trying to get out.
A storm can push extra seawater towards the estuary. If that surge arrives on top of a high tide, the water coming upriver can rise high enough to threaten the streets behind the embankments.

At Woolwich, the barrier crosses five hundred and twenty metres of river. There are ten steel gates. In the main navigation spans, the curved gates rest down on the riverbed, leaving the waterway clear above them.

Deciding to raise them starts well beyond London. Tide gauges measure the sea. Instruments inland track the river. Weather forecasts help the control room estimate how high the water will get, and when it will arrive.
One reading alone cannot tell the controller to close. An ordinary tide with a lot of river water coming down is a different problem from an exceptional tide with very little river water behind it.
Timing is the trick. For a forecast surge, the barrier typically closes just after low tide, about four hours before the peak is expected. By then, much of London's water has already drained out.
Watch one main gate from the side. The curved steel face rotates up out of its recess. Across the navigation opening, the space the ship sailed through is now occupied by a flood barrier.
On the sea side, the tide keeps rising. On the London side, the gate holds that tide back. Fresh water still flows down from upstream, which is why the space left at low tide matters.
Now the sea level begins to fall. Opening too early would let water back towards London. Operators wait until the level on the sea side has fallen to meet the level on the city side.
The gates reopen. Follow the marks on the water this time. They travel out towards the estuary on the falling tide, carrying away the river water that built up while the gates were closed.

Next time you see a ship between those silver piers, picture the gate beneath its keel. London's defence depends on knowing when to lift it, how long to hold it, and when to give the river back its way out.
